blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 11 (Hydrocarbons), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 What are hydrocarbons? Where are they found and what are they used for?
blocks.explanation: Hydrocarbons are organic compounds of only carbon and hydrogen. They are found abundantly in petroleum and natural gas and are used as domestic and industrial fuels; medicines, plastics, perfumes and polymers have their origins in them.

book_ref.quote: They are frequently used as domestic and industrial fuels.

blocks.prompt: 2 Classify aliphatic hydrocarbons into their families, stating whether each is cyclic or acyclic, saturated or unsaturated.
blocks.explanation: Alkanes: acyclic, saturated. Cycloalkanes: cyclic, saturated. Alkenes and alkynes: acyclic, unsaturated. All are aliphatic, i.e. not aromatic.

book_ref.quote: Alkanes are acyclic aliphatic hydrocarbons

blocks.prompt: 3 Why are aromatic compounds called 'aromatic'? Name two derivatives of benzene.
blocks.explanation: The term comes from the Greek word 'aroma' meaning fragrant, because these compounds have a characteristic odour. Benzene (C₆H₆) is the basic aromatic compound; toluene and phenol are its derivatives.

book_ref.quote: The term aromatic was derived from the Greek word

blocks.prompt: 4 Write the general formula of alkanes and use it to write the molecular formulae of alkanes with 9 and 16 carbon atoms.
blocks.explanation: General formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. For n = 9: H = 2(9) + 2 = 20, C₉H₂₀ (nonane). For n = 16: H = 2(16) + 2 = 34, C₁₆H₃₄.

book_ref.quote: Methane (CH₄) is the simplest member of this family.

blocks.prompt: 5 Write the molecular formula and the condensed structural formula of heptane.
blocks.explanation: By CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 7, heptane is C₇H₁₆. Condensed structure: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ (five CH₂ groups between the two CH₃ ends).

book_ref.quote: By CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ heptane is C₇H₁₆

blocks.prompt: 6 What is an alkyl group? How is it named? Give two examples with abbreviations.
blocks.explanation: An alkyl group is what we obtain after removing one hydrogen atom from an alkane. It is named by replacing -ane of the alkane with -yl. Examples: CH₃– methyl (Me–) from methane; CH₃CH₂– ethyl (Et–) from ethane.

book_ref.quote: What we obtain after the removal of one hydrogen atom from an alkane is called an alkyl group.

blocks.prompt: 7 Write the structures and IUPAC names of the four butyl groups.
blocks.explanation: n-Butyl CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂– (butyl); sec-butyl CH₃CH₂CH(–)CH₃ (1-methylpropyl); isobutyl CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂– (2-methylpropyl); tert-butyl (CH₃)₃C– (1,1-dimethylethyl).

book_ref.quote: Table 11.3 alkyl groups, straight chain and branched and their names

blocks.prompt: 8 How is the parent chain of a branched alkane selected and numbered?
blocks.explanation: Select the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms (even if it is bent in the formula); it gives the parent name. Number this chain beginning from the end nearest to the substituent.

book_ref.quote: Number the longest chain beginning from the end nearest to the substituent.

blocks.prompt: 9 Give the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ and state the rule used for identical substituents.
blocks.explanation: Longest chain = 6 carbons (hexane); methyl groups on C-3 and C-4: 3,4-dimethylhexane. Identical substituents are shown by di, tri, tetra and each one gets its own number.

book_ref.quote: Then make certain that each and every substituent has a number.

blocks.prompt: 10 In the name 4-ethyl-2-methylhexane, why is ethyl written before methyl?
blocks.explanation: Substituent groups are listed alphabetically, so ethyl (e) comes before methyl (m), whatever their numbers. Multiplying prefixes such as di and tri are ignored while deciding the alphabetical order.

book_ref.quote: For example, we designate the following compound as 4-Ethyl-2-methylhexane.

blocks.prompt: 11 State the rule used when branching first occurs at an equal distance from either end of the longest chain. Give an example.
blocks.explanation: Choose the name that gives the lower number at the first point of difference. Example: a hexane with methyls numbered 2,3,5 from one end and 2,4,5 from the other is 2,3,5-trimethylhexane (3 is lower than 4).

book_ref.quote: choose the name that gives the lower number at the first point of difference.

blocks.prompt: 12 How are cycloalkanes named? Name the cycloalkanes with three and four ring carbons and write their formulae.
blocks.explanation: The prefix cyclo is attached to the name of the alkane with the same number of carbons. Three ring carbons: cyclopropane, C₃H₆; four: cyclobutane, C₄H₈ (cycloalkanes are CₙH₂ₙ).

book_ref.quote: Cycloalkanes are named by attaching the prefix

blocks.prompt: 13 Why do alkane molecules have a tetrahedral shape around each carbon atom?
blocks.explanation: Each carbon has four sp³ hybridized orbitals forming four single (σ) bonds. The four bonding pairs repel each other equally and point to the corners of a tetrahedron, with bond angles of 109.5°.

book_ref.quote: Alkane molecules have a tetrahedral shape around carbon atoms.

blocks.prompt: 14 State the hybridization, type of bonds, bond angle and C–C bond length in ethane.
blocks.explanation: Each carbon is sp³ hybridized and forms only σ bonds with carbon and hydrogen. Bond angles are 109.5° and the C–C bond length is 1.54 Å.

book_ref.quote: Carbon atoms in alkane molecules form sigma bonds with surrounding carbon and hydrogen atoms.

blocks.prompt: 15 Why are cycloalkanes called saturated? Write the formula of cyclopentane.
blocks.explanation: In cycloalkanes all the ring carbon atoms are singly bonded to other atoms, so they are saturated. They follow CₙH₂ₙ; cyclopentane (five ring carbons) is C₅H₁₀.

book_ref.quote: Cycloalkanes are also saturated, meaning that all of the carbons atoms that make up the ring are singly bonded to other atoms.

blocks.prompt: 16 Describe the physical states of alkanes at room temperature with respect to the number of carbon atoms.
blocks.explanation: Up to four carbons (C₁ to C₄): colourless, odourless gases. Pentane to heptadecane (C₅ to C₁₇): colourless, odourless liquids. C₁₈ onwards: colourless, odourless waxy solids.

book_ref.quote: Alkanes containing upto four carbon atoms are colourless, odourless, gases

blocks.prompt: 17 Why are alkanes insoluble in water but soluble in benzene?
blocks.explanation: Alkanes are non-polar or very weakly polar. So they do not dissolve in polar solvents like water, but dissolve in non-polar solvents such as hexane, benzene and ether.

book_ref.quote: insoluble in polar solvents like water, but soluble in non-polar solvents

blocks.prompt: 18 Which has the higher boiling point, butane or its isomer 2-methylpropane? Give the values.
blocks.explanation: Butane (straight chain) boils higher, at -0.50 °C; 2-methylpropane (isobutane, branched) boils at -11.7 °C. Branched alkanes boil lower than their normal-chain isomers.

book_ref.quote: The boiling points of alkanes having branched chain structures are lower than their isomeric normal chain alkanes

blocks.text: 11.3 Reaction mechanism and modes of bond breaking

blocks.prompt: 19 What is meant by reaction mechanism? In how many ways can a covalent bond break?
blocks.explanation: Reaction mechanism is the series of steps that take place in the course of the overall reaction. Organic reactions involve breaking of bonds; a covalent bond can break in two ways: homolytic and heterolytic fission.

book_ref.quote: Reaction mechanism is the series of steps that take place in the course of the overall reaction.

blocks.prompt: 20 What is a free radical? Why are free radicals extremely reactive?
blocks.explanation: A free radical is a species that contains an unpaired electron, formed by homolytic fission. It is extremely reactive because the unpaired electron tends to become paired.

book_ref.quote: Free radicals are extremely reactive because of the tendency of unpaired electrons to become paired.

blocks.prompt: 21 Show the homolytic fission of a chlorine molecule. What is formed?
blocks.explanation: Cl–Cl → Cl• + Cl•. The covalent bond breaks evenly, each atom keeping one electron of the shared pair, so two chlorine free radicals are formed.

book_ref.quote: Figure 11.5: Homolytic fission and free radical formation

blocks.prompt: 22 Show the heterolytic fission of the C–Cl bond of a chloroalkane. How is it shown in mechanisms?
blocks.explanation: R₃C–Cl → R₃C⁺ + Cl⁻. The shared pair is gained by chlorine only, giving a carbocation and a chloride ion (oppositely charged ions). It is shown by a full curly arrow.

book_ref.quote: Figure 11.6: Heterolytic fission and formation of ions

blocks.text: 11.4 Unreactive nature of alkanes towards polar reagents

blocks.prompt: 23 Why are alkanes called paraffins?
blocks.explanation: Paraffin comes from Latin parum = little and affinis = affinity. Alkanes have little affinity (reactivity): they are inert towards acids, alkalis, oxidizing and reducing agents under ordinary conditions.

book_ref.quote: parum = little, affinis = affinity

blocks.prompt: 24 How does electronegativity explain the inertness of alkanes towards polar reagents?
blocks.explanation: C = 2.5 and H = 2.1 differ by only 0.4, so the bonding electrons in C–H and C–C are almost equally shared. The bonds are almost non-polar, giving polar reagents no charged site to attack.

book_ref.quote: The electronegativity values of carbon (2.5) and hydrogen (2.1) do not differ appreciably

blocks.prompt: 25 How does the nature of the sigma bond make alkanes unreactive?
blocks.explanation: In a sigma bond the electrons are very tightly held between the nuclei, making it a very stable bond. A lot of energy is required to break it, so alkanes react only under high temperature or suitable conditions.

book_ref.quote: A lot of energy is required to break it.

blocks.prompt: 26 What harmful effects can the combustion of hydrocarbons have on the environment?
blocks.explanation: Combustion produces CO₂, a greenhouse gas contributing to climate change. Incomplete combustion can release carbon monoxide (CO) and particulate matter, with serious health and environmental consequences.

book_ref.quote: Hydrocarbon combustion produces CO₂, a greenhouse gas contributing to climate change.

blocks.prompt: 27 Name the two types of reactions that alkanes undergo under high temperature or suitable conditions.
blocks.explanation: (1) Thermal and catalytic reactions, e.g. combustion and cracking. (2) Free radical substitution reactions, in which an atom or group of atoms is replaced by another through the free radical mechanism (e.g. halogenation).

book_ref.quote: Under high temperature or suitable conditions, alkanes undergo two types of reactions.

blocks.prompt: 28 What is halogenation of alkanes? Under what conditions does it occur?
blocks.explanation: Halogenation is the substitution of hydrogen atoms of an alkane by halogen atoms through free radicals. Alkanes react with chlorine and bromine in sunlight or UV light; the hydrogens are replaced one after another, the extent depending on the amount of halogen.

book_ref.quote: An example is the substitution of a halogen atom with a hydrogen of an alkane, called halogenation.

blocks.prompt: 29 Give reasons: (i) fluorine is not used for direct halogenation of alkanes; (ii) iodine does not substitute alkanes directly.
blocks.explanation: (i) The reaction with fluorine is highly violent and gives a mixture of carbon, fluorinated alkanes and hydrofluoric acid. (ii) With iodine the reaction is too slow and reversible. Reactivity: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.

book_ref.quote: Iodine does not substitute directly because the reaction is too slow and reversible.

blocks.prompt: 30 Write the initiation and propagation steps for the chlorination of ethane in UV light.
blocks.explanation: Initiation: Cl–Cl → 2Cl• (UV light). Propagation: CH₃–CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃–CH₂• + HCl, then CH₃–CH₂• + Cl–Cl → CH₃–CH₂Cl + Cl•. The new Cl• carries the chain forward.

book_ref.quote: Propagation step is the second step in the free radical substitution

blocks.prompt: 31 Write the three ways in which the termination step can occur in the chlorination of methane.
blocks.explanation: (i) •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl (chloroalkane). (ii) Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂. (iii) •CH₃ + •CH₃ → CH₃–CH₃ (an alkane with double the carbon atoms, formed in traces). In each, two free radicals combine.

book_ref.quote: The termination may take place in different ways.

blocks.prompt: 32 Why is the presence of traces of ethane in the chlorination of methane taken as evidence of the free radical mechanism?
blocks.explanation: Ethane (double the carbon atoms of methane) can form only when two methyl free radicals merge in a termination step. This termination is rare, so ethane appears in traces, but its presence proves that methyl radicals were formed.

book_ref.quote: This type of termination is rare and the alkanes with double carbon atoms are formed in traces.

blocks.prompt: 33 Write the successive substitution products of methane with excess chlorine, with their names.
blocks.explanation: CH₄ → CH₃Cl (chloromethane) → CH₂Cl₂ (dichloromethane) → CHCl₃ (trichloromethane, chloroform) → CCl₄ (tetrachloromethane, carbon tetrachloride); HCl forms at each step. More chlorine gives more highly chlorinated products.

book_ref.quote: Successive substitution of chloromethane to tetrachloromethane

blocks.prompt: 34 Why is the use of haloalkanes as solvents in the laboratory strictly monitored?
blocks.explanation: Haloalkanes are anaesthetic and toxic; their anaesthetic power increases with the number of halogen atoms. So their use as organic solvents in the lab is strictly monitored.

book_ref.quote: Use of these as organic solvents in lab is strictly monitored due to their toxic nature.

blocks.prompt: 35 Why are alkenes called unsaturated hydrocarbons? Write the molecular formula of the alkene with six carbon atoms.
blocks.explanation: Their molecules contain a carbon to carbon double bond, and they have two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding saturated hydrocarbon. Hexane is C₆H₁₄, so the alkene is C₆H₁₂ (hexene).

book_ref.quote: Alkenes have two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding saturated hydrocarbons.

blocks.prompt: 36 Give the IUPAC names of (i) CH₃–CH₂–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ (ii) (CH₃)₂CH–CH=CH₂.
blocks.explanation: (i) Seven-carbon chain numbered from the end nearer the double bond, which starts at C-3: 3-heptene. (ii) Four-carbon chain containing C=C, numbered from the CH₂= end; CH₃ on C-3: 3-methyl-1-butene.

book_ref.quote: The IUPAC rules for naming alkenes are similar in many respects to those for naming alkanes.

blocks.prompt: 37 Write the structural formulae of (i) 3-methyl-1-pentene (ii) 2-methyl-1-butene.
blocks.explanation: (i) CH₂=CH–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃. (ii) CH₂=C(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₃. In each, C-1 and C-2 form the double bond and the methyl group sits on the carbon given by its number.

book_ref.quote: Number the chain so as to include both carbon atoms of the double bond.

blocks.prompt: 38 What are elimination reactions? How are they used to prepare alkenes?
blocks.explanation: In elimination reactions small atoms (H, OH, X) are removed from adjacent carbon atoms of a saturated compound, i.e. a small molecule such as H₂O or HCl is lost, creating a C=C double bond. Ethene is made this way from ethanol and from ethyl bromide.

book_ref.quote: In such reactions, a small molecule such as H₂O or HCl, is removed from adjacent carbons in an organic molecule.

blocks.prompt: 39 Write the two steps of the preparation of ethene from ethanol and concentrated H₂SO₄.
blocks.explanation: Step 1: CH₃–CH₂OH + H₂SO₄ → CH₃–CH₂–OSO₃H (ethyl hydrogen sulphate) + H₂O (180°C). Step 2: CH₃–CH₂OSO₃H → H₂C=CH₂ + H₂SO₄ (heat).

book_ref.quote: In the first step, ethyl hydrogen sulphate is formed which decomposes on heating to produce ethene.

blocks.prompt: 40 Differentiate between dehydration of alcohols and dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides.
blocks.explanation: Both are elimination reactions giving alkenes; they differ in the starting compound, reagent and the molecule removed.

book_ref.quote: The reaction involves the removal of a water molecule from the alcohol molecule.

rows: Starts from an alcohol, e.g. ethanol.
Starts from an alkyl halide, e.g. ethyl bromide.
Reagent: excess concentrated H₂SO₄, 180°C.
Reagent: alcoholic KOH, on heating.
A water molecule is removed.
Hydrogen and halogen (as KBr + H₂O) are removed.
CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O
H₃C–CH₂–Br + KOH → H₂C=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O

blocks.prompt: 41 Write any four physical properties of alkenes.
blocks.explanation: (1) Ethene, propene and butene are gases; C₅ to C₁₅ are liquids; higher members are solids. (2) Insoluble in water but soluble in alcohol. (3) Characteristic smell; burn with a luminous flame. (4) Weakly polar, unlike alkanes, because of sp² hybridization.

book_ref.quote: First three members i.e. ethene, propene and butene are gases at room temperature

blocks.prompt: 42 Describe the hybridization of each carbon atom in ethene.
blocks.explanation: Each carbon mixes its 2s orbital with two 2p orbitals to form three equivalent sp² hybrid orbitals lying in one plane. One unhybrid p-orbital is left, perpendicular (90°) to that plane.

book_ref.quote: Ethene (C₂H₄) is the simplest alkene.

blocks.prompt: 43 How is the π bond formed in ethene?
blocks.explanation: The unhybrid p-orbitals of the two carbon atoms are parallel to each other and overlap laterally (sideways). This lateral overlap forms the second carbon-carbon bond, the π bond, above and below the plane of the σ bonds.

book_ref.quote: The unhybrid p-orbitals of each carbon atom which are parallel to each other overlap laterally to form another carbon-carbon bond.

blocks.prompt: 44 Why is the ethene molecule planar?
blocks.explanation: sp² hybridization gives a trigonal planar arrangement around each carbon with bond angles of about 120°. The two double-bond carbons and the four atoms attached to them lie in the same plane.

book_ref.quote: The sp² hybridization results in a trigonal planar arrangement around each carbon atom.

blocks.prompt: 45 Differentiate between a σ bond and a π bond.
blocks.explanation: The σ bond forms by linear overlap and is strong; the π bond forms by lateral overlap and is weaker.

book_ref.quote: A π bond is, therefore, a weak bond as compared to a σ-bond.

rows: Formed by linear (end-to-end) overlap, e.g. of sp² orbitals.
Formed by lateral overlap of parallel unhybrid p-orbitals.
Electrons lie on the line joining the two nuclei.
Electrons lie away from the line joining the two nuclei.
Electrons tightly held; strong, stable bond.
Electrons less firmly held; weak bond, breaks easily.
Present in alkanes and alkenes.
Present in alkenes (the second bond of C=C).

blocks.prompt: 46 Why are alkenes more reactive than alkanes?
blocks.explanation: Alkenes have a double bond containing a π bond. The π electrons lie away from the internuclear line, are less firmly held and break easily; they are also exposed to attack by electrophiles, so alkenes undergo electrophilic addition easily.

book_ref.quote: Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes due to the presence of the double bond.

blocks.prompt: 47 Why do alkenes act as nucleophiles?
blocks.explanation: A nucleophile (Nu:⁻) donates a pair of electrons. Alkenes contain loosely held π electrons which they can donate to an electrophile (E⁺), so they act as nucleophiles.

book_ref.quote: Alkenes act as nucleophile because they contains pi electrons.

blocks.prompt: 48 What is the role of ethene in the ripening of fruits?
blocks.explanation: Plants produce ethene as a natural ripening hormone. For efficient harvesting and transport, fruits and vegetables are picked unripe and exposed to ethene so that they ripen in a short time.

book_ref.quote: fruits and vegetables are often picked unripe

blocks.prompt: 49 What is a carbocation? Classify CH₃CH₂⁺, (CH₃)₂CH⁺ and (CH₃)₃C⁺.
blocks.explanation: A carbocation is an alkyl group with a single positive charge on one carbon atom. CH₃CH₂⁺: primary (1°), bonded to one carbon; (CH₃)₂CH⁺: secondary (2°), two carbons; (CH₃)₃C⁺: tertiary (3°), three carbons.

book_ref.quote: Carbocations are classified into following types.

blocks.prompt: 50 Arrange CH₃⁺, CH₃CH₂⁺, (CH₃)₂CH⁺ and (CH₃)₃C⁺ in increasing order of stability.
blocks.explanation: CH₃⁺ < CH₃CH₂⁺ < (CH₃)₂CH⁺ < (CH₃)₃C⁺. Stability increases with the number of electron-donating (+I) alkyl groups on the positive carbon, so the tertiary carbocation is the most stable.

book_ref.quote: This means that tertiary carbocation is the most stable

blocks.prompt: 51 Differentiate between the positive (+I) and negative (-I) inductive effects.
blocks.explanation: Both polarize a σ bond; +I groups donate electrons, -I groups withdraw them.

book_ref.quote: Electron donating species, are said to have positive inductive effect(+I)

rows: Shown by electron donating groups.
Shown by electron withdrawing groups.
Example: alkyl groups.
Example: a halogen atom.
Pushes electrons towards a positive carbon, stabilizing a carbocation.
Pulls bonded electrons; carbon becomes partial positive.
Makes the carbocation less positive.
Creates a permanent dipole, halogen negative.

blocks.prompt: 52 Why is a carbocation an electrophile?
blocks.explanation: A carbocation carries a positive charge on a carbon atom, so it is an electron pair acceptor (electrophile). It reacts with a nucleophile, e.g. Br⁻, which gives it an electron pair.

book_ref.quote: Due to the positive charge on the carbon atom, carbocation is electrophile.

blocks.prompt: 53 Explain the -I effect of chlorine in a chloroalkane C₂–C₁–Cl.
blocks.explanation: Chlorine withdraws the bonded electrons, so it becomes partial negative and C₁ partial positive (δ⁺). The effect passes along the chain, so C₂ carries a smaller positive charge (δδ⁺). A permanent dipole arises.

book_ref.quote: Electron withdrawing groups, such as a halogen atom, have a negative inductive effect (-I).

blocks.prompt: 54 What is electrophilic addition? Outline its general mechanism.
blocks.explanation: It is the addition of an electrophile to the double bond of an alkene. The electron-rich C=C attacks the electrophile X⁺, giving a carbocation intermediate; the nucleophile Y⁻ then attacks the carbocation to give the addition product.

book_ref.quote: Alkenes reacts with an electrophile to give a carbocation intermediate that then reacts with a nucleophile.

blocks.prompt: 55 How is the unsaturation of an organic compound tested with bromine? Give the equation with ethene.
blocks.explanation: Bromine (red-brown) is added to the compound in an inert solvent like carbon tetrachloride; an unsaturated compound discharges the colour at once. CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → Br–CH₂–CH₂–Br.

book_ref.quote: Halogenation means addition of halogens like chlorine or bromine.

blocks.prompt: 56 Br₂ is non-polar. How does it act as an electrophile towards an alkene?
blocks.explanation: When Br₂ comes close to the C=C, the high electron density of the double bond repels the Br–Br electron pair away from the nearer Br. That Br atom becomes slightly positive (δ⁺) and acts as the electrophile; it accepts a pair of π electrons.

book_ref.quote: Bromine (Br₂) is a non-polar molecule

blocks.prompt: 57 Write the steps of the mechanism of addition of HBr to ethene.
blocks.explanation: Step 1: the nucleophilic π bond attacks the H of H–Br; HBr gives Br⁻ and ethene becomes the carbocation CH₃–CH₂⁺. Step 2: Br⁻ (nucleophile) attacks the carbocation: CH₃–CH₂–Br (bromoethane).

book_ref.quote: Nucleophilic pi-bond attacks the hydrogen in hydrogen halide.

blocks.prompt: 58 State Markovnikov's rule and predict the main product of adding HBr to 2-methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂.
blocks.explanation: Rule: when a polar reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the negative part attaches to the double-bonded carbon bearing fewer hydrogens. H adds to CH₂, giving the 3° carbocation (CH₃)₃C⁺; Br⁻ then gives (CH₃)₃C–Br, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

book_ref.quote: When a polar reagent adds to an unsymmetrical alkene

blocks.prompt: 59 Arrange HF, HCl, HBr and HI in the order of their rate of addition to alkenes. On what does the product depend?
blocks.explanation: Rate: HF < HCl < HBr < HI (the rate increases from HF to HI). All add across C=C the same way; the product depends on whether the alkene is symmetrical (one product) or unsymmetrical (two possible products).

book_ref.quote: All hydrogen halides (HBr,HCl,HI,HF) give this reaction

blocks.prompt: 60 What is hydrogenation? Give its conditions and its industrial use.
blocks.explanation: Hydrogenation is the addition of molecular hydrogen to an alkene with a Ni/Pt catalyst at 250-300 °C to form a saturated compound: H₂C=CH₂ + H₂ → H₃C–CH₃. Industrially it converts vegetable oil into margarine (Banaspati ghee).

book_ref.quote: Hydrogenation means addition of molecular hydrogen to an alkene

blocks.prompt: 61 Differentiate between hydrogenation and hydration of ethene.
blocks.explanation: Hydrogenation adds H₂ and gives an alkane; hydration adds H₂O and gives an alcohol.

book_ref.quote: Similar to hydrohalogenation, the alkene forms a carbocation intermediate

rows: Addition of molecular hydrogen (H₂).
Addition of water (steam).
Catalyst Ni/Pt at 250-300 °C.
Concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst, high temperature and pressure.
Product: ethane, H₂C=CH₂ + H₂ → H₃C–CH₃.
Product: ethanol, H₂C=CH₂ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH.
Used to make margarine from vegetable oil.
Goes through a carbocation, attacked as in hydrohalogenation.

blocks.prompt: 62 What is halohydration? Write the equation for ethene with bromine water and name the product.
blocks.explanation: Halohydration is the reaction of an alkene with a halogen in the presence of water to form a halohydrin. H₂C=CH₂ + Br₂ + H₂O → Br–CH₂–CH₂–OH + HBr; the product is 2-bromoethanol (ethylene bromohydrin).

book_ref.quote: Br and OH add to the two carbons of the double bond

blocks.prompt: 63 What is an epoxide? How is ethylene oxide obtained from ethene and what does its acid hydrolysis give?
blocks.explanation: An epoxide is an oxygen-containing three-membered cyclic ether formed by epoxidation of an alkene. Ethene is converted to ethylene oxide using molecular oxygen and a transition metal catalyst. Acid hydrolysis converts the epoxide into a diol.

book_ref.quote: Ethene can also be converted to ethylene oxide using molecular oxygen and metal catalysts.

blocks.prompt: 64 What is ozonolysis? Write the equation for ethene and state one use of the reaction.
blocks.explanation: Ozonolysis is the oxidative cleavage of alkenes by ozone (O₃): the alkene forms an ozonide, which is reduced to carbonyl compounds. C₂H₄ + O₃ → C₂H₄O₃ →(Zn/H₂O) 2CH₂O. It is used to identify the structure of unknown alkenes.

book_ref.quote: Alkenes react with ozone (O₃) to form ozonides

blocks.prompt: 65 Differentiate between a monomer and a polymer.
blocks.explanation: Monomers are the small reactive molecules; polymers are the extremely long molecules they form.

book_ref.quote: Polymerization is the formation of extremely long molecules (polymers) from small reactive molecules that join together (monomers).

rows: A small reactive molecule.
An extremely long-chain molecule.
Contains at least one C=C (for addition polymers).
Has only C–C single bonds in the chain.
Example: ethene, CH₂=CH₂.
Example: poly(ethene), made of many repeating units.
Example: chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl.
Example: PVC.

blocks.prompt: 66 What is a repeating unit? Write the equation for the polymerization of chloroethene showing the repeating unit.
blocks.explanation: A repeating unit is the smallest group of atoms that, connected one after another, makes up the polymer chain; it is shown in square brackets. n CH₂=CHCl → [–CH₂–CHCl–]ₙ (PVC); the C=C of the monomer becomes a C–C single bond.

book_ref.quote: A repeating unit is the smallest group of atoms that when connected one after the other make up the polymer chain.

blocks.prompt: 67 Name two conjugated dienes and write their structures.
blocks.explanation: But-1,3-diene: CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂. 2-Methylbut-1,3-diene (isoprene): CH₂=C(CH₃)–CH=CH₂. In each, the two C=C are separated by one single bond.

book_ref.quote: As the name indicates, a diene is a molecule containing two double bonds between carbon atoms.

blocks.prompt: 68 Is CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH=CH₂ a conjugated diene? Give a reason.
blocks.explanation: No. In a conjugated diene the double bonds are separated by one single bond. Here a CH₂ group lies between them, so they are separated by two single bonds and their p-orbitals cannot overlap over the whole system.

book_ref.quote: In a Conjugated diene, the double bonds in the carbon chain are separated by a single bond.

blocks.prompt: 69 Give one industrial use of 1,3-butadiene and explain why it is suitable.
blocks.explanation: 1,3-Butadiene is used in the production of synthetic rubber. Its conjugated structure allows polymerization, giving long chains that show rubber-like properties.

book_ref.quote: The conjugated structure allows for polymerization, leading to long chains that exhibit rubber-like properties.

blocks.prompt: 70 Why is isomerism common in hydrocarbons with more than three carbon atoms? How many isomers does pentane have?
blocks.explanation: With more than three carbons the atoms can be arranged in more than one way while satisfying all valencies, so different structures share one molecular formula. The number of isomers rises rapidly with carbon number; pentane has three.

book_ref.quote: Isomerism is not only possible but common if the compound contains more than three carbon atoms.

blocks.prompt: 71 Write the chain isomers of butane (C₄H₁₀) with their names.
blocks.explanation: CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ (butane, straight chain) and CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₃ (2-methylpropane, isobutane, branched). They differ in the nature of the carbon chain.

book_ref.quote: for pentane (C₅H₁₂) and butane (C₄H₁₀), the following arrangements are possible.

blocks.prompt: 72 Differentiate between chain isomerism and position isomerism.
blocks.explanation: Chain isomers differ in the carbon chain; position isomers have the same chain but the group is at a different position.

book_ref.quote: This type of isomerism arises due to the difference in the nature of the carbon chain.

rows: Arises from a difference in the nature of the carbon chain.
Arises from a different position of the same functional group.
The carbon skeleton changes (straight or branched).
The arrangement of carbon atoms remains the same.
Example: butane and 2-methylpropane.
Example: but-1-ene and but-2-ene.
Example: pentane and its branched isomers.
Example: 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane.

blocks.prompt: 73 What is functional group isomerism? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different functional groups show functional group isomerism. Example: C₂H₆O is ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH (alcohol), and methoxymethane, CH₃–O–CH₃ (ether).

book_ref.quote: The compounds having the same molecular formula but different functional groups are said to exhibit functional group isomerism.

blocks.prompt: 74 What is metamerism? Give an example of a pair of ethers that are metamers.
blocks.explanation: Metamerism arises from unequal distribution of carbon atoms on either side of the functional group; the metamers belong to the same homologous series. Example: ethoxyethane CH₃CH₂–O–CH₂CH₃ and methoxypropane CH₃–O–CH₂CH₂CH₃, both C₄H₁₀O.

book_ref.quote: unequal distribution of carbon atoms on either side of the functional group

blocks.prompt: 75 What is tautomerism? Give the example described in the chapter.
blocks.explanation: Tautomerism arises from the shifting of a proton from one atom to another in the same molecule. Amino acids exist as zwitterions, formed when a proton shifts from the carboxylic acid end to the amine group.

book_ref.quote: They exist as zwitterions which are formed when a proton is shifted from the carboxylic acid end

blocks.prompt: 76 Differentiate between structural isomerism and stereoisomerism.
blocks.explanation: Structural isomers differ in the arrangement of atoms; stereoisomers have the same structural formula but differ in space.

book_ref.quote: The structural isomerism arises due to the difference in the arrangement of atoms within the molecule.

rows: Arises from a difference in the arrangement of atoms within the molecule.
Same structural formula; identical groups differ in their positions in space.
Structural formulas are different.
Structural formulas are the same.
Five types: chain, position, functional group, metamerism, tautomerism.
Two types: geometrical (cis-trans) and optical.
Studied in this chapter.
Part of the Class 12 syllabus.

blocks.prompt: 77 Differentiate between organic oxidation and organic reduction.
blocks.explanation: Organic oxidation adds oxygen or removes hydrogen; organic reduction adds hydrogen or removes oxygen.

book_ref.quote: During organic reduction, hydrogen is added or oxygen is removed.

rows: Oxygen is added or hydrogen is removed.
Hydrogen is added or oxygen is removed.
Example: C₂H₅OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O.
Example: H₂C=CH₂ + H₂ → H₃C–CH₃ (Pt).
Agents: acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, O₃, O₂ with metal catalysts.
Agents: LiAlH₄, NaBH₄, Sn + conc. HCl.
Also: combustion, ozonolysis, epoxidation.
Also: carboxylic acid to primary alcohol, nitrobenzene to phenylamine.

blocks.prompt: 78 Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethane. Why is it an organic oxidation?
blocks.explanation: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → 4CO₂ + 6H₂O (or C₂H₆ + 7/2 O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O). Check: C 4 = 4, H 12 = 12, O 14 = 8 + 6. Oxygen is added to carbon and hydrogen, so it is an oxidation.

book_ref.quote: Oxidation of organic compounds involving reaction with oxygen is usually the combustion reaction:

blocks.prompt: 79 Name three reducing agents used in organic synthesis and write the reduction of ethanal.
blocks.explanation: LiAlH₄, NaBH₄ and Sn + conc. HCl. With LiAlH₄ on heating: CH₃–CHO + 2[H] → CH₃–CH₂–OH (ethanal to ethanol); hydrogen is added, so it is a reduction.

book_ref.quote: Various reducing agents are used in Organic synthesis.

blocks.prompt: 80 Write the equation for the oxidation of ethanol by acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. Why is it called oxidation?
blocks.explanation: C₂H₅OH + 2[O] → CH₃COOH + H₂O. The primary alcohol becomes a carboxylic acid (ethanoic acid); oxygen is added and hydrogen removed, so it is an oxidation.

book_ref.quote: Reaction of primary alcohols with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ to make carboxylic acids

blocks.prompt: 81 Why is the epoxidation of an alkene classed as an oxidation reaction?
blocks.explanation: In epoxidation an oxygen atom is added across the C=C of the alkene, forming a three-membered cyclic ether (epoxide). Addition of oxygen is organic oxidation; oxidizing agents such as molecular oxygen with metal catalysts are used.

book_ref.quote: The epoxidation of alkene is also example of oxidation reaction.
